title: Spring Boot
description: The framework that makes building Java APIs and services fast, with REST and database integration.
resumo: Spring Boot = Spring + starters + auto-configuration + an embedded server (Tomcat).
IoC: the container creates the beans. Inject through the constructor; with one constructor, `@Autowired` is not needed.
`@RestController` returns objects that Jackson turns into JSON; `@Service` holds the rules; Spring Data builds queries from method names.
Input: DTO (record) + Bean Validation + `@Valid` gives an automatic 400. Never expose the JPA entity.
Errors: `@RestControllerAdvice` in one place; `ProblemDetail` standardizes the body.
Configuration: `application.yml`, overridden by environment variables; secrets never in the file.

subsections.subtitle: What Is Spring Boot?
subsections.description: Spring with sensible defaults and an embedded server.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** plain Spring needs a lot of setup before the first endpoint: a web server, the dispatcher, a data source, JSON conversion, and library versions that work together.

**Concept:** Spring Boot sits on top of the Spring Framework. Starters are dependency bundles with versions tested together; auto-configuration creates beans based on what is on the classpath and in your properties; an embedded server (Tomcat) makes the application a runnable JAR.

**How it works:** generate a project at start.spring.io, add starters, write code. `@SpringBootApplication` combines `@Configuration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration` and `@ComponentScan`, which scans the main class's package and its subpackages.
examples.code:
<!-- pom.xml: one starter brings Spring MVC, Jackson and Tomcat -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

@SpringBootApplication
public class ShopApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ShopApplication.class, args);
    }
}

$ ./mvnw spring-boot:run      # or: ./mvnw package && java -jar target/shop.jar
examples.interview_question: Why is Spring Boot preferred for building modern APIs?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Putting the main class in a package that does not contain the others. Component scanning only looks at the main class's package and below it, so controllers and services elsewhere are never found.

subsections.subtitle: Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection
subsections.formerSubtitle: Inversão de Controle e Injeção de Dependência
subsections.description: Spring creates the objects and wires them together.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** `OrderService` does `new PaymentClient()` inside itself. It cannot be tested without calling the real payment provider, and the implementation cannot be swapped.

**Concept:** with inversion of control, the Spring container creates and connects the objects (beans) instead of your code calling `new`. With dependency injection, a class receives its dependencies, usually through the constructor. Beans are found by annotations (`@Service`, `@Component`) or declared with `@Bean` in a `@Configuration` class.

**How it works:** prefer constructor injection: the dependencies are explicit, the fields can be `final`, and a unit test can pass mocks without starting Spring. With a single constructor, `@Autowired` is not needed. Avoid `@Autowired` on fields, which hides dependencies.
examples.interview_question: What are IoC and dependency injection, and why prefer constructor injection?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Two beans of the same type and a constructor that asks for "the" one. Spring cannot choose and fails at startup. Pick one with `@Qualifier`, or mark a default with `@Primary`.

subsections.subtitle: Core Annotations
subsections.description: Telling Spring what each class is.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** Spring needs to know what each class is — a controller, business logic, data access — to create it and apply the right behavior.

**Concept:** `@Component` is a generic bean; `@Service` holds business logic; `@Repository` is data access (and translates database exceptions into Spring's `DataAccessException`); `@Controller` serves web pages; `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody`, returning data as JSON. `@Configuration` with `@Bean` declares beans by hand.

**How it works:** in controllers, `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping` (and the other verbs) map URLs to methods; `@PathVariable` reads a part of the path, `@RequestParam` a query parameter and `@RequestBody` the JSON body.
examples.interview_question: What does @RestController do, and how is it different from @Controller?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Using `@Controller` for an API. Spring treats the returned String as the name of a view template, so the request fails instead of returning the text or JSON.

subsections.subtitle: Spring MVC
subsections.description: How a request travels from URL to JSON.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every HTTP request has to be read (URL, parameters, JSON body), routed to the right code and turned back into a response with a status and a body.

**Concept:** in Spring MVC, the `DispatcherServlet` receives every request, finds the matching method (`@GetMapping`...), converts the parameters and the body, calls the method and converts the return value to JSON. The conversion is done by an `HttpMessageConverter` (Jackson). In a REST API no view is involved.

**How it works:** a request flows client → DispatcherServlet → controller → service → repository, and back. Return the object for a plain 200, or a `ResponseEntity` to control the status and headers.
examples.interview_question: How does Spring MVC handle a REST request, from URL to JSON?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Business logic in the controller. Rules, database access and HTTP get mixed, and the rules cannot be reused or tested without HTTP. The controller translates HTTP; the service holds the rules.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every entity needs the same CRUD code — save, find by id, list, delete — plus queries by some field.

**Concept:** you declare an interface that extends `JpaRepository<Entity, Id>`, and Spring generates the implementation at startup: `save`, `findById`, `findAll`, `deleteById`, paging. Derived queries turn a method name into a query (`findByEmail`, `findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter`). `@Query` takes JPQL when the name would get too long.

**How it works:** keep queries in the repository and let the database do the filtering, sorting and paging.
examples.interview_question: How do you create a custom query with Spring Data JPA?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Calling `findAll()` and filtering in Java. The whole table is loaded into memory for a few rows. Let the database filter.

subsections.subtitle: Configuration Properties
subsections.description: Values that change per environment, outside the code.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the database URL, the port and timeouts differ between your machine, test and production. Hard-coded values mean a new build per environment.

**Concept:** Spring Boot reads configuration from `application.properties` or `application.yml`, environment variables and command-line arguments; later sources override earlier ones, so an environment variable beats the file. Relaxed binding maps `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` to `spring.datasource.url`.

**How it works:** keep defaults in the file and override per environment with environment variables. Read values with `@Value`, or group them with `@ConfigurationProperties` (Intermediate level).
examples.code:
# application.yml
server:
  port: 8080
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
    username: shop
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}        # from an environment variable
shop:
  free-shipping-above: 200.00

@Value("${shop.free-shipping-above}")
private BigDecimal freeShippingAbove;

$ SERVER_PORT=9090 java -jar shop.jar      # the environment variable overrides the file
examples.interview_question: How does Spring Boot load configuration, and how do you override a value per environment?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A typo in a property name. Spring does not complain: the value is simply not applied, and the default is used. `@ConfigurationProperties` with validation, or the IDE's property completion, catches it.
examples.code:
# WRONG: "datasorce" — ignored silently; the app tries the default database
spring:
  datasorce:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop

# RIGHT
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you want to check the controller — JSON, status code, validation — without starting the server by hand and clicking through Postman after every change.

**Concept:** `spring-boot-starter-test` brings JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ and MockMvc. `@SpringBootTest` loads the whole application. MockMvc sends simulated HTTP requests through Spring MVC without a real server. Slices load only one layer: `@WebMvcTest` (controllers) and `@DataJpaTest` (repositories). `@MockitoBean` replaces a bean with a mock.

**How it works:** for a controller, `@WebMvcTest` with the service mocked is the usual choice: it checks routing, JSON and validation, and starts much faster than the full application.
examples.interview_question: How do you test a REST endpoint with MockMvc, and when do you use @WebMvcTest instead of @SpringBootTest?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Using `@SpringBootTest` for every test. The whole application — database connection included — starts again and again, and the suite gets slow. Use slices for one layer, and keep `@SpringBootTest` for a few end-to-end checks.

subsections.subtitle: Data Validation
subsections.description: Rejecting invalid input before it reaches the service.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a client sends an empty name or an invalid email. Without validation it reaches the database, or breaks a rule deep inside the code.

**Concept:** Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation, from `spring-boot-starter-validation`) declares rules as annotations: `@NotNull`, `@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Email`, `@Min`, `@Positive`, `@Pattern`. `@Valid` on the controller parameter triggers the check, and a failure becomes a 400 Bad Request.

**How it works:** put the rules on the request DTO. `@NotBlank` rejects null, empty and whitespace; `@NotNull` only null. A nested object is validated only if its field also has `@Valid`.
examples.interview_question: How do you make sure an endpoint's input is valid?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Annotations that are never checked: `@Valid` missing on the parameter, or the validation starter missing from the project. Nothing fails — the invalid data just goes through.
examples.code:
// WRONG: without @Valid the annotations on the record are ignored
public ResponseEntity<UserResponse> create(@RequestBody CreateUserRequest req) { ... }

<!-- Also required: without this dependency nothing is validated -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
</dependency>

subsections.subtitle: Exception Handling in APIs
subsections.description: One place that turns exceptions into HTTP responses.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an order that does not exist should be a clear 404, not a 500 with a stack trace. And a try/catch in every controller is repetitive and inconsistent.

**Concept:** the service throws domain exceptions; a `@RestControllerAdvice` class with `@ExceptionHandler` methods turns each type into a response, in one place for the whole API. `ProblemDetail` (RFC 9457) gives the error body a standard format.

**How it works:** map each expected exception to its status (404, 400, 409), and let a final handler turn anything unexpected into a generic 500, with the details only in the log.
examples.interview_question: How do you centralize error handling in a Spring Boot API?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Using `@ControllerAdvice` (without "Rest") and returning a String. Like `@Controller`, it treats the String as a view name, so the error handler itself fails. Use `@RestControllerAdvice`.

subsections.subtitle: Spring Security Basics
subsections.description: Authentication and authorization with a filter chain.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** right after adding the dependency, every endpoint returns 401. You need some public routes, others only for logged-in users, and some only for admins.

**Concept:** Spring Security runs as a chain of filters before your controller. Authentication answers "who are you?" and authorization "what can you do?". You configure a `SecurityFilterChain` bean that says which paths are public and which need a login or a role.

**How it works:** adding `spring-boot-starter-security` protects everything and logs a generated password for a default user — fine for a first try, never for production. Rules are checked in order, so specific paths come first and `anyRequest()` last. APIs usually authenticate with tokens (JWT), covered in the advanced level.
examples.interview_question: How do you protect endpoints with Spring Security?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Putting `anyRequest()` before the specific rules. The rules are evaluated in order, and Spring refuses this configuration at startup.

subsections.subtitle: DTOs and Mapping
subsections.description: Do not expose JPA entities in the API.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** returning entities ties the API contract to the database model. A new column changes the JSON, sensitive fields can leak, and lazy relationships fail during serialization.

**Concept:** a DTO (Data Transfer Object) defines exactly what enters and leaves the API, separately from the entity. Records are a good fit: immutable, short, and easy to validate. Request and response DTOs can differ per use case.

**How it works:** map entity to DTO in the service or with a static factory method (`from`). The entity can change freely as long as the mapping keeps the contract.
examples.interview_question: Why use DTOs instead of returning JPA entities from controllers?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Returning the entity directly. Every field goes to the client — including the password hash — and lazy relationships throw `LazyInitializationException` or trigger extra queries while Jackson serializes them.
